properties.state: {"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-08. Nothing here is intent and nothing has been chosen. THE IDEA, his words: allocation of functions to systems/services could be driven by what the system is for — \"maybe you allocate functions based on it being fault tolerant or very highly reliable or easily maintainable or based on maximal performance\" — and the agent would deduce the likely answer and then ASK (\"is this design about performance or reliability or maintainability or highly secure\"), because \"answering that question really determines how you allocate functions to which services\" and \"if you don't ask upfront, these cost a lot in having to rework services after they've been already developed\". It follows an earlier thought of his in the same conversation: that allocation could be decided by graph theory alone — Leiden communities for clustering, or PageRank to avoid bottlenecks and god nodes — with domain-oriented and function-oriented decomposition \"thrown out the window\". WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, checked rather than assumed: the `dimension` enum in schema/dimensions.yaml already carries reliability, performance, maintainability, security, scalability, observability, testability, coupling and maturity, attachable to ANY node; `propose_allocation` already clusters the weighted capability graph with Leiden and never auto-applies; `evaluate_allocation` already computes modularity, misplaced capabilities and god-components as selective articulation points; and `ility_report` (BL-184, from Anthony's own correction on 2026-08-03) already maps those computations onto the axis each one informs, emitting named findings and never a score. SO THE DIRECTION IS THE NEW PART: everything above runs GRAPH → ILITY, reading structure and saying what it implies. This idea runs ILITY → GRAPH, stating the attribute and letting it drive the allocation. Same vocabulary, opposite direction of inference, and that direction does not exist. AN OBSERVATION WORTH KEEPING WHATEVER IS DECIDED: the attribute may change not just the OBJECTIVE FUNCTION but WHICH GRAPH IS BUILT. Performance wants the call-frequency / data-volume graph and minimal cross-boundary chatter, which is what Leiden on DEPENDS_ON.weight already does. Reliability wants no articulation points and may deliberately DUPLICATE a function across services so one failure domain cannot take everything — which directly OPPOSES maximal modularity, since a modularity-optimal partition is often reliability-hostile. Maintainability wants things that change together to live together, which is a CO-CHANGE graph, a different edge set entirely. Security wants boundaries following trust and data classification with some nodes separated regardless of coupling — constrained partitioning, not clustering at all. Four attributes, four different graphs over the same functions; any single \"run Leiden and allocate\" answer silently picks performance. THE ONE THAT IS RUNNABLE TODAY, and it is a cheap falsifiable experiment: maintainability. reflow2 already holds 316 ChangeEvents with CHANGED edges, which IS a co-change graph, already populated, needing no instrumentation — cluster it and diff against evaluate_allocation's current map to see whether things that change together are allocated together. Performance is NOT runnable: evaluate_allocation reports total_internal 1, total_external 0, unweighted_dependencies 1 — one capability-to-capability dependency edge in the whole design, unweighted, which is why modularity reads a meaningless 1.00. Reliability and security have no substrate at all yet. COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, recorded beside the idea rather than used to argue it down: (1) a service boundary carries obligations no coupling graph encodes — deployment unit, failure domain, team ownership, release cadence, data residency, regulatory scope — so two functions Leiden puts together may belong apart because one is audited and one is not, and no resolution parameter can see that; (2) this project has already paid twice for metric-driven verdicts, retiring `unexpected_coupling` because it fired on correct architecture (\"that coupling IS the product\") and accepting SPOFs deliberately in dec:sanitize-spof-accepted and dec:service-spof-accepted, so a purely metric-driven allocator would flag all three and be wrong each time; (3) clustering on ESTIMATED weights is an opinion with extra steps and a modularity score on top, which is worse than the opinion because it looks objective — the schema's own weight_basis (estimated / evidence / measured) exists to keep that distinction visible. WHERE THE IDEA IS STRONGEST, narrower than \"replace the old methods\": it makes allocation ARGUABLE. Today domain-versus-function is unfalsifiable and the louder voice wins; computing modularity, bottleneck centrality and cross-boundary weight for candidate allocations turns it into evidence — which is the shape register_alternative / analyze_alternatives already have, with dec:parallel-alternatives putting AoA alternatives in design-space via CONTRADICTS.","name":"OPEN — does the quality attribute a system is FOR decide how functions are allocated, and does each attribute need its own graph?","rationale":"Recorded under the brainstorm skill so the thinking survives without being claimed as intent. Three things make it worth keeping even if none of it is built: the ility-to-graph direction is genuinely absent while its whole vocabulary is present; the four-graphs observation would change what any future allocation feature computes rather than merely how it weights; and the co-change experiment is runnable today on data already in the graph, which makes at least one branch falsifiable now instead of after instrumentation. The counter-arguments are recorded beside rather than against — an idea killed in conversation loses its reasoning, an idea recorded with its objection keeps both.","status":"proposed"}
